question.prompt:
Problems \(8,\) \(9,\) and \(10\) use the data found in the accompanying paragraph and figures.

Bake Sale

Four friends, Art, Roger, Paul and Trisha, bake cookies, and all cookies have the same thickness. The shapes of the cookies differ, as shown.

• Art’s cookies are trapezoids:

[Figure 1](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig1.svg)

• Roger’s cookies are rectangles:

[Figure 2](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig2.svg)

• Paul’s cookies are parallelograms:

[Figure 3](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig3.svg)

• Trisha’s cookies are triangles:

[Figure 4](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig4.svg)

Each friend uses the same amount of dough, and Art makes exactly \(12\) cookies.

Art’s cookies sell for \(60\)¢ each. To earn the same amount from a single batch, how much should one of Roger’s cookies cost?

solutions.explanation:
Equal amounts of dough at the same thickness give Art's and Roger's batches the same total cookie area. Their individual cookie areas, in square inches, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Art: }&\frac{(3+5)\cdot3}{2}=12,\\
\text{Roger: }&4\cdot2=8.
\end{aligned}
\]
Art makes \(12\) cookies, so each batch has total cookie area \(12\cdot12=144\) square inches. Roger therefore makes \(144\div8=18\) cookies.

Art's batch earns \(12\cdot60=720\) cents. To earn the same total from Roger's \(18\) cookies, the price of each must be
\[
720\div18=40\text{ cents}.
\]
Roger should charge \(40\)¢ per cookie, choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
solutions.title: Find the batch size and revenue
